lessons.t: What is A.I., really?
lessons.th: Test everything; hold on to what is good. That is the whole class in one verse.
lessons.b: An LLM is a very well-read helper that guesses the next word. It can sound completely sure and still be wrong. It is a tool — not a source of truth.
lessons.p: Your AI Sounds Certain. Should You Trust It?
lessons.d: This lesson explains that a large language model is a pattern-guesser that predicts the next word, so it can produce confident answers that are simply made up. It shows why a wise user treats AI as a powerful tool to be steered carefully,…

lessons.t: Asking good questions
lessons.th: Answering before you listen is folly — and so is asking before you think.
lessons.b: A clear question gets clear help. The four keys: what, when, why, how. Garbage in, garbage out — but a good question is a kind of skill.
lessons.p: Why Your A.I. Answers Feel Vague: The Question Is the Real Lever
lessons.d: This lesson shows how a clear question shapes the quality of an A.I. answer, using four keys: what you want, when or where it applies, why you need it, and how you want it returned. It also explains how giving the model a role and audience…

lessons.t: The Test — judging what A.I. tells you
lessons.th: The filter for what is worth keeping in your mind: true, honorable, just, pure, lovely.
lessons.b: The most important week. Never trust an answer just because it sounds smart. Run it through the filter and VERIFY it. AI that looks right and is wrong is the real danger.
lessons.p: Why Does an AI Answer That Sounds Right Deserve the Most Doubt?
lessons.d: This lesson shows why a wrong answer that looks convincing is more dangerous than an obviously wrong one, and how to run AI output through a standard of truth before repeating it. It teaches a simple habit: check any factual claim against…

lessons.t: A.I. for school — honestly
lessons.th: Daniel mastered Babylon’s learning without losing who he was. Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart.
lessons.b: Use it to LEARN, not to cheat. It is your tutor, not your ghostwriter. The goal is a stronger you, not a shortcut that leaves you weaker.
lessons.p: Is A.I. Making You Smarter or Quietly Replacing Your Thinking?
lessons.d: This lesson shows the difference between using A.I. to learn and using it to cheat, and why the test is whether you end up stronger. It draws on Daniel's example of using a system in Babylon without being owned by it, and on the call to do…

lessons.t: A.I. that serves people
lessons.th: Whoever wants to be great must serve. Use your freedom to serve one another in love.
lessons.b: The best use of this tool is to help someone else. Use the app to serve the church — prayer requests, trivia, helping an elder use their phone.
lessons.p: What If the Smartest Thing You Do With AI Is Help Someone Else?
lessons.d: This lesson shows how to point your AI skills outward, using them to serve others like writing a prayer request with an elder or helping a grandparent send a photo. It also explains how teaching a phone-shy elder deepens your own understan…

lessons.t: Build something useful
lessons.th: Do you see someone skilled in their work? They will stand before kings.
lessons.b: You are a builder, not just a user. Make one small useful thing — a scripture-memory helper, a study buddy, a chore tracker.
lessons.p: Could You Build the Next Helpful App Yourself? Start Smaller Than You Think
lessons.d: This lesson shows the difference between simply using technology and making something with it, and why a good prompt, a clear plan, and one small useful tool count as real building. It encourages you to start with a modest project, such as…

lessons.t: Guarding your heart and your time
lessons.th: Do not be mastered by anything; guard your heart.
lessons.b: A tool this powerful pulls at your attention, your privacy, and your sense of what is real. Set your limits before you need them — wisdom is knowing when to put it down.
lessons.p: Who Gets Your Heart When the Screen Gets Your Time?
lessons.d: This lesson names four pulls of a powerful AI tool: over-reliance, time loss, oversharing, and trusting a screen more than people and Yahweh. It shows how to set guardrails in advance, deciding what you will never share and when you will s…

lessons.t: Teach the next group
lessons.th: Entrust what you learned to faithful people who will teach others.
lessons.b: The best students help teach the next group. You have grown from user, to discerner, to server, to maker — now to multiplier. Kings raise kings.
lessons.p: Who Are You Ready to Teach, and What Would You Hand Them First?
lessons.d: This commissioning lesson looks back over the eight-week path from user to discerner, server, maker and now multiplier, and asks you to prepare a five-minute lesson on the week that helped you most. It shows that teaching something simply…

lessons.t: The whole chain — sanctuary to the world
lessons.th: One body, many members. The eye can’t say to the hand "I don’t need you." Every station matters; the broadcast is a body, not a stack of gear.
lessons.b: The broadcast is one chain: camera → capture → OBS → encode → stream → screens. Every person here is one link. A chain is only as strong as its weakest link — and only as strong as the team praying it on.
lessons.p: What Breaks First When a Church Broadcast Goes Dark? Tracing the Whole Path From Pulpit to Screen
lessons.d: This lesson walks through the full path a church broadcast travels, from camera and capture card through OBS, the encoder, and the stream to the screens in the Sanctuary and at home. It shows how each volunteer hands their work to the next…

lessons.t: The camera and the image — Chris’s 4K eye
lessons.th: "The light of the body is the eye" (Matthew 6:22), and the eyes are told to look right on (Proverbs 4:25). A clean, well-aimed image serves everyone watching.
lessons.b: The camera is where the picture is born — get it wrong here and nothing downstream can fix it. Chris runs the main 4K Blackmagic on the Sanctuary; that one feed is what the room AND the Bishop see, so everyone is looking at the same thing.
lessons.p: Why Does One Camera Decide What the Whole Room Sees?
lessons.d: This lesson explains why the camera is where every broadcast picture begins, and why problems there cannot be fixed later in the chain. It also shows why the main 4K feed is shared with both the Sanctuary screens and the Bishop's monitor,…

lessons.t: Light — Isaiah and Coreyon make it seeable
lessons.th: The first thing God made was light. Let your light shine before others so they see good works and glorify the Father. Light is where creation — and the image — begins.
lessons.b: The camera can only capture the light you give it. Light is not decoration — it is the raw material of the whole image. Isaiah and Coreyon control whether the room reads as warm and clear, or flat and dim, on every screen.
lessons.p: Can a Camera Show Truth Without Enough Light?
lessons.d: This lesson shows how a camera only records the light it receives, so controlling light decides whether a room looks clear and warm or dark and flat. It follows Isaiah and Coreyon as they shape clean, even light on the pulpit and keep the…

lessons.t: OBS and the switch — Bradley runs the look
lessons.th: Let all things be done decently and in order. The switch is where order either shows or breaks — a calm, intentional cut serves the worshipper; a frantic one distracts them.
lessons.b: OBS is the control room in software. A "scene" is a saved arrangement of cameras, slides, and lower-thirds; "switching" is cutting between scenes live. Bradley owns the look of the broadcast — calm, intentional cuts, never frantic.
lessons.p: Who Decides What the Congregation Sees, and When? Inside the Director's Chair
lessons.d: This lesson explains how OBS works as a software control room, where a scene is a saved arrangement of sources and switching is cutting between scenes live. It shows why calm, anticipated cuts on natural beats help a service feel carried,…

lessons.t: The machines — CPU, GPU, CUDA, and the two 4070s
lessons.th: God filled Bezalel with skill and ability to work in every craft and to teach others. Mastering the tools of the trade — and understanding them — is a Spirit-given calling, not just a technical one.
lessons.b: The left and right machines that drive the Sanctuary screens run on RTX 4070 GPUs — graphics cards, not "cpus." A CPU is a few powerful workers doing one hard job at a time; a GPU is thousands of small workers doing the same math all at once. That difference is why 4K and A.I. are even possible.
lessons.p: Why Does a Graphics Card Do in One Second What a Processor Takes Its Time On?
lessons.d: This lesson clears up the confusion over the two RTX 4070 machines that drive the Sanctuary screens, explaining why they are graphics cards rather than CPUs. It breaks down how a CPU handles a few hard tasks at once while a GPU runs thousa…

lessons.t: The pipes — 4K bandwidth and the network
lessons.th: Which of you, wanting to build a tower, doesn’t first sit down and count the cost — whether you have enough to finish? Plan the capacity before you build the broadcast on it.
lessons.b: Raw 4K video is enormous — about 12 billion bits every second, uncompressed. No normal internet can send that. The network and the cables are the pipes; if a pipe is too small, the picture stutters. Knowing NVMe vs Cat6 vs 10-gig keeps the broadcast flowing.
lessons.p: Why Does a 4K Picture Need Bigger Pipes Than Your Internet Can Carry?
lessons.d: This lesson shows how much data raw 4K video creates and how NVENC compression shrinks it to a size the internet can send. It also untangles NVMe storage, Cat6 Ethernet, and SDI cable so you can tell which pipe does what and why an undersi…

lessons.t: A.I. that serves the broadcast — and how it really works
lessons.th: Test everything; hold fast what is good. Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly. A.I. is a tool to spread the Word further — never a source of truth to trust unchecked.
lessons.b: An A.I. like an LLM is a very well-read helper that guesses the next word — it can sound sure and be wrong, so we test it. Used wisely, it serves the broadcast: live captions, turning the Bishop’s sermon into clips and notes, and searching the whole sermon archive (The Word — Migdal) by meaning.
lessons.p: Can an AI Tool Make Our Broadcast Better Without Making Things Up?
lessons.d: This lesson explains why an AI language model can sound certain while being wrong, and how a church broadcast team can use it safely for live captions, sermon drafts, and searching the Bishop's sermon archive by meaning. Every draft and ev…

lessons.t: Capturing the Work: POV SOPs
lessons.th: Write the vision; make it plain on tablets, so the one who reads it may run. Tell the next generation the works of the Lord. Plain, recorded instruction is how the work is handed on.
lessons.b: We record each station’s real procedure first-person with the Ray-Ban Meta glasses, and the church’s own A.I. turns it into a written checklist. Tacit "you just have to know" skill becomes a transferable SOP — so the next person can run with it. We capture the team and the gear, never the congregation.
lessons.p: What If the Best Way to Pass On Your Skill Is Just Recording Yourself at Work?
lessons.d: This lesson shows how the team can capture each station's real procedure first-person with Ray-Ban Meta glasses, then have the church's own local A.I. draft a written checklist that a person corrects before it goes into the SOP Library. It…

lessons.t: Excellence as worship — and raising the next operators
lessons.th: Whatever you do, work heartily as for the Lord and not for men. What you have heard, entrust to faithful people who can teach others. Excellence is worship; the work is handed on.
lessons.b: We hold a high standard because the broadcast is worship and it carries the Word — not to impress anyone, but because it’s for the King. The mark of mastery is that you make it reliable, and that you can teach the next person. Founders raise founders.
lessons.p: Why Does a Sunday Broadcast Need to Work Every Single Week, and Who Learns It Next?
lessons.d: This lesson explains why the church broadcast team holds a high standard: the broadcast is an act of worship that carries the Word to people who depend on it, so excellence means being reliable every Sunday through a written run-of-show an…

lessons.t: Own the iron — what "sovereign infrastructure" means
lessons.th: Put in the garden to work it and keep it; it is required of stewards that they be found faithful. We own and tend the iron as stewards, not as owners who extract.
lessons.b: Sovereign means we own the machines our data and our A.I. run on, instead of renting someone else’s. See the whole map: the home stack and the church stack. We own the iron so it serves the family and the community — never the other way around.
lessons.p: Who Really Holds the Keys to Your Family's Photos and Your Church's Sermons?
lessons.d: This lesson explains sovereign infrastructure as owning and governing the machines that run your data, automation, and A.I., at home and at church, instead of renting space on a distant company's computers. It also shows the honest respons…

lessons.t: The brain and the barn — the Synology NAS
lessons.th: Joseph stored up grain in the storehouses against the lean years; the wise store up choice provision. The NAS is our storehouse — what we save now protects us later.
lessons.b: The NAS is one box that does two big jobs: it STORES the family’s data (the barn) and it RUNS our services and local A.I. (the brain). It’s a serious server — a Xeon CPU, error-correcting memory, many drive bays — but on purpose it has no graphics card.
lessons.p: One Box, Two Jobs: Why Your Home Server Stores the Family's Data and Runs Its Helpers
lessons.d: This lesson shows how the Synology NAS works as a barn that safely stores family data across drive bays and as a brain that runs automation, local A.I., sharing and alerts. It also explains why the box has no graphics card on purpose, and…

lessons.t: Never lose the family’s data — disks, RAID, and backups
lessons.th: Know well the state of your flocks; count the cost before you build. Knowing what you have, and protecting it, is wisdom — not fear.
lessons.b: Hard drives WILL fail eventually — so we plan for it. RAID lets the NAS keep working when one drive dies. And a backup is a second copy somewhere else: 3 copies, 2 kinds of media, 1 offsite. We keep an encrypted copy at the church, sealed.
lessons.p: If Every Hard Drive Will Eventually Fail, What Keeps Your Family's Photos Safe?
lessons.d: This lesson explains why RAID and backups are two different protections: RAID keeps a NAS running when one drive dies, while a backup is a separate copy kept somewhere else. It walks through the 3-2-1 rule, the value of test restores, and…

lessons.t: Walls and gates — the UniFi gateway
lessons.th: Come, let us rebuild the wall; they prayed and set a guard day and night. Walls and a watch are how a city — and a network — stays safe and whole.
lessons.b: The network gateway is the front door of the whole system AND the inside walls. It connects us to the internet, and it splits the network into separate rooms (VLANs) so the family, the church, the clinic, the rentals, and PoeTech each stay walled off from the others.
lessons.p: Who Gets to Walk Through Your Front Door, and Who Stays in Their Own Room?
lessons.d: This lesson shows how one network gateway acts as both the front door to the internet and the interior walls that split a shared system into separate rooms, so family, church, clinic, rentals and PoeTech each stay protected. It also covers…

lessons.t: Reaching it safely from anywhere — Tailscale & WireGuard
lessons.th: The gatekeeper opens to the shepherd; the Lord keeps your going out and coming in. The right door opens only for the right ones — that is safety, not suspicion.
lessons.b: We need to use the stack from the road without leaving the front door wide open to the world. A private tunnel (VPN) like Tailscale or WireGuard lets the right people in over an encrypted path — and keeps everyone else out. The app reaches the NAS the same private way.
lessons.p: How Do You Reach Your Home Server From the Road Without Opening the Door to Everyone?
lessons.d: This lesson explains how a private encrypted tunnel, such as Tailscale built on WireGuard, lets trusted devices reach the family NAS from anywhere while keeping the public out. It also previews the plan to give limited access to outside pe…

lessons.t: Our own A.I. — Ollama and the models on our hardware
lessons.th: Test everything; hold fast what is good — for the Lord gives wisdom. Our A.I. is a tool to be tested, and true wisdom comes from God, not the machine.
lessons.b: We run A.I. on OUR machines, so the family’s and the church’s words never go to a stranger’s cloud. Ollama runs open models on the NAS. Because the NAS is CPU-only, it runs SMALL models — fine for many jobs, and the bigger ones wait for the GPU box (week 7).
lessons.p: Can a Home A.I. Run Without Sending Your Family's Words to a Stranger?
lessons.d: This lesson shows how Yahweh-minded stewardship can guide running language models on your own NAS with Ollama, so family and church words stay home. You will also see the limits of small CPU-only models, why heavier work waits for a GPU bo…

lessons.t: Why we’re building a GPU farm — CPU vs GPU and VRAM
lessons.th: God filled Bezalel with skill to work every craft; and count the cost before you build. Knowing the tools — and sizing them honestly — is a Spirit-given, sober calling.
lessons.b: A GPU (a graphics card) has thousands of tiny workers doing the same math at once — exactly what big A.I. needs. The catch is VRAM (the GPU’s own memory): a 70-billion-parameter model needs about 48 GB of it. The NAS has none, so a dedicated GPU box is planned. The church’s video-wall machines (RTX 4070s) are our real…
lessons.p: Why Does a 70B AI Model Need 48 GB of Memory on One Card?
lessons.d: This lesson explains why a GPU's thousands of small cores suit AI work, and why a model's weights must fit inside the card's own VRAM, which a 70-billion-parameter model needs about 48 GB to hold. It also shows, plainly and honestly, what…

lessons.t: The house of God — COLG’s sovereign stack
lessons.th: Be strong and do the work; do not be afraid — God is with you until it is finished. Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain. We build the house for Him.
lessons.b: The Church of the Living God built a 33,000 sq ft house, serves the largest African American community in Champaign-Urbana, and couldn’t find tech support — so we build it ourselves. The church stack mirrors the home stack: a sovereign NAS, the LED video wall + 4070 machines, and the broadcast — all serving the first…
lessons.p: Who Builds a Church's Tech When No One Else Will?
lessons.d: This lesson shows how The Church of the Living God in Champaign-Urbana, a 33,000-square-foot house serving its largest African American community, gets its own sovereign tech stack: a NAS, the Sanctuary LED video wall, and the broadcast ch…

lessons.t: Keeping it alive — health, alerts, and the three brakes
lessons.th: Who then is the faithful and wise manager? They prayed and set a watch day and night. Watchfulness — a watch that never sleeps — is faithful stewardship.
lessons.b: Owning the iron means keeping it healthy. The system watches itself: health checks on every workflow, push alerts (ntfy) so it tells YOU when something’s wrong, and the in-app health cards that read live. And any automation that runs on a timer carries three brakes so it can never run away.
lessons.p: Who Notices First When Your System Breaks, and What Stops It From Running Away?
lessons.d: This lesson shows how a home system can watch itself with health checks, ntfy push alerts that reach your phone at high priority when something fails, and live in-app health cards that report "not connected" or "stale" rather than guessing…

lessons.t: Build it right — and raise the next builders
lessons.th: Entrust what you’ve learned to faithful people who can teach others; whatever you do, work heartily as for the Lord. The work is handed on, and it’s done for Him.
lessons.b: Sovereignty is stewardship: we build to a high standard because the family and the church depend on it, and we hand it on. You truly own a part of the stack when you can teach it. Founders raise founders — and the media team builds and runs BOTH infrastructures.
lessons.p: Can You Teach It? The Test That Proves You Really Own the Build
lessons.d: This commissioning lesson ties the course together under stewardship: build to a high standard because family and church depend on it, make it reliable with written checklists and recorded sequences, and prove ownership by teaching one oth…

lessons.t: The generator in the garage — why local-first
lessons.th: The wise build on rock that holds when the storm comes; the prudent see danger and take refuge. Owning the foundation our tools run on is that kind of wisdom — not fear.
lessons.b: A company that hosts your A.I. can change its policy, raise its price, go down, or cut you off — and if your family’s and church’s tools live only on its servers, they go dark with it. Local-first A.I. is a generator in the garage: when the grid flickers, our lights stay on. We build sovereign by default, and we never…
lessons.p: What Happens to Your A.I. the Day a Provider Pulls the Plug?
lessons.d: This lesson explains why Yahweh-minded families and churches might run their most important A.I. on hardware they own, rather than renting it from a provider that can change terms, raise prices, go down, or cut off access. It also shows th…

lessons.t: What a model costs to run — size, capability, hardware
lessons.th: Count the cost before you build; by wisdom a house is built and by knowledge its rooms are filled. Sizing a tool honestly to the job is stewardship.
lessons.b: A model’s SIZE (its parameter count) drives what it can do AND what hardware it needs. Bigger is generally more capable but needs more memory and is slower. "Quantization" shrinks a model to fit smaller hardware, trading a little quality for a lot of reach. The honest chain is: size → capability → hardware → what to e…
lessons.p: Bigger Isn't Always Better: How Much Does Your AI Really Cost to Run?
lessons.d: This lesson walks through the honest chain of size, capability, hardware, and what to expect when running a model locally. You'll see how parameter count and quantization shape memory needs and speed, and why picking the smallest model tha…

lessons.t: The model-tier landscape — what runs where
lessons.th: God gave Bezalel skill for every craft; there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit. Different tools for different work, each honored for what it does.
lessons.b: There isn’t one "A.I." — there’s a landscape of models at different sizes, and a matching landscape of hardware tiers to run them. Three tiers: the AI Forge tier (a GPU / Mac Studio node — deep logic, RAG, agentic work), the Synology-CPU tier (the DS1621xs now — small quantized models), and the deep-reasoning tier (fr…
lessons.p: Not All A.I. Runs on the Same Box: Which Model Fits Which Machine?
lessons.d: This lesson shows that "A.I." is really a range of models at very different sizes, and that each needs a matching hardware tier. It walks through the three tiers we use: the Synology-CPU box we run today for small models, the planned GPU n…

lessons.t: The honest ceiling — what small CPU models can and can’t do
lessons.th: Test everything; the prudent give thought to their steps. We test the tool against the task instead of trusting a label.
lessons.b: Running A.I. on a CPU-only box is real and useful — but it has an honest ceiling. Small quantized models are slow on the CPU NAS and weaker on long, complex personas and deep multi-step reasoning. Knowing the ceiling is what keeps us honest: we use small models for what they’re good at, and route the rest up.
lessons.p: Where Does a Small AI Model Hit Its Limit, and What Should You Do Then?
lessons.d: This lesson shows where a small, CPU-only local AI model is honestly limited: slow long outputs, weaker multi-step reasoning and persona consistency, and limited use of long context. It also shows where such a model excels, and why routing…

lessons.t: How SKOS runs it — Ollama, routing, and the Cage
lessons.th: A person without self-control is like a city with broken walls; who then is the faithful manager? Brakes and walls are what make power safe to wield.
lessons.b: SKOS runs local models with Ollama, routes each task to the right tier (small local first; a vendor only for heavy lifting), grounds answers in our own corpus with a RAG pipeline, and keeps every autonomous step behind the Cage — the brakes. Sovereign-walled work (private/family/clinical) is local-only, always.
lessons.p: Who Decides Where Your A.I. Work Runs, and What Keeps It From Running Off?
lessons.d: This lesson shows how the SKOS system runs A.I. on hardware the team owns through Ollama, routes each task to the right tier, and grounds answers in its own corpus with RAG. It also explains the Cage, the walls and brakes that keep automat…

lessons.t: Vendor vs local — the honest trade-offs
lessons.th: Plans are established by counsel; there is a time for everything. Wisdom is matching the work to the right tool at the right time.
lessons.b: Local isn’t always right and vendor isn’t always wrong. Vendors win on frontier reasoning, very-long context, and multimodal (image / video / audio — e.g., a vendor for video understanding). Local wins on privacy, resilience, always-on cost, and sovereignty. The skill is matching the work to the right mind — and never…
lessons.p: Which AI Should Handle Your Work? Matching Each Task to the Right Mind
lessons.d: This lesson explains where vendor AI models excel, such as deep reasoning, very long documents, and video or audio understanding, and where local models excel, such as privacy, resilience, and steady low-cost routine work. It shows how to…

lessons.t: The five local-A.I. opportunities — the strategy
lessons.th: What you did for the least of these, you did for Me; good news to the poor, freedom for the captive. Serving the overlooked is the mission, and here it is also the market.
lessons.b: Sovereign A.I. isn’t just safer for us — it’s a market the extractive giants can’t serve. Five opportunities: (1) regulated industries, (2) data-never-leaves tools, (3) air-gapped agents, (4) zero-internet environments, and (5) resilience-as-a-service. Each is a place where "your data never leaves and your tool can’t…
lessons.p: Where Could Your Local A.I. Be the Only Tool That Still Works?
lessons.d: This lesson walks through five places where a sovereign, locally run A.I. meets real need: regulated industries, data-never-leaves tools, air-gapped agents, zero-internet environments, and resilience-as-a-service. It also shows how the sam…

lessons.t: Build it sovereign — and hand it on
lessons.th: Entrust what you’ve learned to faithful people who can teach others; whatever you do, work heartily as for the Lord. The understanding is handed on, and it’s done for Him.
lessons.b: Sovereignty is stewardship: we build A.I. on iron we own because the family and the community depend on it, we tell the truth about what it can and can’t do today, and we hand the understanding on. You own this when you can teach it. The roadmap is honest — the GPU tier is planned, not pretended — and the work outlast…
lessons.p: Could You Explain Your Home A.I. to Someone Who Wasn't There?
lessons.d: This commissioning lesson ties the whole Sovereign A.I. course together around stewardship: building on hardware we own, being honest about what runs today versus what is only planned, and passing the understanding on so others can carry i…

lessons.t: Why verification matters in the age of A.I. — trust is earned, never claimed
